The three neural subsystems underlying visual attention are separable from early infancy.

how attention develops and how this relates to the development of visual attention.
the development of visual attention from birth to 6 years of age.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural substrates of attentional control are present in the first year of life, and the ability to use them develops rapidly during the first five years.

attentional disorders are associated with a wide range of developmental syndromes, and that the early identification of such attentional deficits may be a critical step in the remediation of these disorders.
attentional disorders are a major cause of developmental disorders and that the early detection of such disorders would allow for the early implementation of appropriate interventions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the study of typical and atypical development of attention in early childhood has revealed a rich and complex system of attentional control that is critical for normal development and that is vulnerable to a range of disorders.
attention develops in three stages: first, the ability to disengage and shift attention; second, the ability to maintain attention; and third, the ability to control attention.
attentional disorders in the first years are associated with specific developmental disorders of the dorsal cortical visual stream.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of attention is not unitary but is made up of three distinct neural subsystems, each of which is critical for the child's ability to function in the world.
attention is not a single unitary process but is composed of multiple neural subsystems, which develop at different rates.
attention is an important aspect of the development of cognitive competence in young children and is a promising early indicator of developmental disorders.
